awd_titl_txt: Conference: Rice Spring School on Electron Correlation and Topology
awd_abstract_narration:
This award is co-funded by the Condensed Matter and Materials Theory, and the Condensed Matter Physics programs of the Division of Materials Research. It will support the attendance of early-career researchers and students to the 2025 instance of the Rice Spring School on Electron Correlation and Topology. The school will bring together leading theorist and experimentalist experts in cutting-edge areas of condensed matter physics to present pedagogical lectures, which will provide graduate students and postdoctoral researchers with a comprehensive understanding of exciting developments and foster new insights into the frontiers of research in quantum materials. The school will also provide a platform for students and early-career researchers to take on active roles as organizers, lecturers, presenters, and panel discussion leaders.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Recent years have highlighted the exciting potential that emerges when strong electron correlations intertwine with the topology of electronic wavefunctions. The central goal of the 2025 Rice Spring School on Electron Correlations and Topology—the second iteration of this school series—was to address critical and emerging problems at this intersection, which is driving some of the most intellectually active directions in quantum condensed matter physics. The school brought together leading theorists and experimentalists to deliver pedagogical lectures and discussions, equipping graduate students and postdoctoral researchers with a coherent understanding of recent advances and open questions in quantum materials research.

The 2025 school attracted more than 80 participants and covered a broad range of topics, including correlated systems; novel topological material platforms for realizing topological flat-band systems; theoretical modeling of correlated topology; emerging experimental probes; quantum entanglement in strongly correlated matter; and out-of-equilibrium many-body dynamics. Designed primarily for junior researchers, the program included structured professional-development opportunities such as a poster competition, contributed talks and student-led discussions, allowing participants to practice scientific communication and leadership while receiving direct feedback from experts. To extend the impact beyond the in-person meeting, we publicized the event through university communications and recorded lecture content for online sharing as reusable educational resources. Together, these outcomes strengthen the pipeline of young scientists working at the interface of correlations and topology and broaden access to high-level training in quantum materials research.
